name: perf_sweep
result: batch 32=29s/10步, 64=57s/10步 -> 吞吐恒定271K tok/s (compute-bound); no_grad_ckpt NaN -> 根因见 850369a
hypothesis: Where is SFT throughput going, and why does disabling activation checkpointing produce NaN?
finding: Throughput is compute-bound at ~271K tok/s across 6 H20s — doubling the batch doubles step time exactly, so batch tuning is a dead end. The NaN has nothing to do with FP8 range (input amax 936 against an e4m3 limit of 448, scaling correct): Inductor's min-cut partitioner recomputes FP8LinearFunction's saved fp8 tensors in the backward graph, re-dividing already-scaled values. Isolated by bisection — eager is clean at batch 2 and 8 with Muon and 130 steps; adding torch.compile NaNs at step 1 with a finite forward and all 152 parameter gradients NaN.
decision: @torch._dynamo.disable on FP8Linear.forward (commit 850369a); verified 60 clean steps with compile on and grad_ckpt off. Activation checkpointing can now be dropped for roughly 25% more speed. Stop tuning batch size for throughput.

name: sft_v3
hypothesis: Does 489K verified rows from open Chinese datasets (Ape210K, Belle, Mxode, math23k) beat the baseline?
finding: No — 26.8%, a regression. Ape210K was 32% of the mix and its rows are a single line ('列式：5/3 = 1.667') with no intermediate steps. Average generation fell to 136 characters and the model started answering division with quotient-and-remainder where the gold answer is a fraction. A large share of one-line data actively destroys multi-step reasoning.
decision: Cap any single-line source at roughly 10% of the mix. Judge a math corpus by the step count of its solutions, not by its row count.

name: sft_v4
hypothesis: With Ape210K capped at 10% and openo1/s1k restored, does 2.4x the loss tokens of v3 beat the 32.2% baseline?
finding: Recovered the regression (32.0%) but did not beat the baseline, despite 175M loss tokens against v3's 72M. Three runs now sit within 0.2 points of 32%: this is a plateau, not noise. Generation is clean (132 chars, 89.6% boxed) and still arithmetically wrong. The corpus is also less diverse than its row count suggests — deduplication dropped 126K of Mxode's 220K rows as Belle prompts rewritten.
decision: Stop adding data drawn from the same distribution. Next: (a) the L3/L4 hard eval set, to establish whether 32% is a model ceiling or holdout saturation, since all 500 holdout problems come from Belle; (b) genuinely heterogeneous data — TinyGSM's 11.8M rows are MIT-licensed and share no distribution with Belle; (c) drop grad_ckpt now that the NaN cause is fixed, for ~25% faster iteration.

name: sft_v5
finding: Adding 76.7K program-generated rows (756 programs) on top of v4 changed nothing: 31.0% vs v4 32.0%, within noise. Four runs now sit at 31-32%. Also confirmed the FP8 NaN fix in production: grad_ckpt off ran 1150 steps with zero NaN at 393K tok/s vs 271K with it (+45%).
decision: Stop iterating on this holdout ��� it is saturated. Judge future runs on math_hard_eval_1k (same ckpt scores 0.8% there). Next levers are architecture (AttnRes from aupai-05) and genuinely out-of-distribution data (TinyGSM), not more same-distribution rows.

notes: AttnRes A/B at equal tokens, torchao FP8, 6xH20
hypothesis: Does Attention Residuals (softmax over depth) lower pretrain loss at equal tokens, and what is the torchao FP8 throughput vs 393K tok/s on the legacy path?

name: rlvr_gspo
notes: GSPO seq-level ratio+clip, KL anchor to frozen SFT ref, degenerate-group filtering, T=0.9; base ckpt_sft_v5 (math-500 31.0%, math-hard 3.1%)
hypothesis: The first RLVR run collapsed 32%->11%. Do the three identified causes explain it: T=0.1 zero-variance groups, no KL anchor, and forced-EOS padding inside the loss mask? With T=0.9, a k3 KL anchor, sequence-level GSPO clipping, and generations truncated at their own EOS, does RL now lift a 3.1% hard-eval model instead of destroying it?

name: rlvr_gspo
notes: GSPO seq-level ratio+clip, KL anchor to frozen SFT ref, degenerate-group filtering, T=0.9; base ckpt_sft_v5 (math-500 31.0%, math-hard 3.1%)
hypothesis: The first RLVR run collapsed 32 to 11 percent. Do the three identified causes explain it: T=0.1 zero-variance groups, no KL anchor, and forced-EOS padding inside the loss mask? With T=0.9, a k3 KL anchor, sequence-level GSPO clipping, and generations truncated at their own EOS, does RL lift a 3.1 percent hard-eval model instead of destroying it?
result: aborted: duplicate launch shared port 29540 and one log file
finding: A pod-side nohup keeps running even when the local tool call is rejected right after, so the first launch was already live; the retry died on EADDRINUSE and both wrote the same log.

name: rlvr_gspo2
notes: GSPO seq-level ratio+clip, k3 KL anchor to the frozen SFT ref, degenerate-group filtering, T=0.9; base ckpt_sft_v5 (math-500 31.0%, math-hard 3.1%)
hypothesis: The first RLVR run collapsed 32 to 11 percent. Do the three identified causes explain it: T=0.1 zero-variance groups, no KL anchor, and forced-EOS padding inside the loss mask? With T=0.9, a k3 KL anchor, sequence-level GSPO clipping, and generations truncated at their own EOS, does RL lift a 3.1 percent hard-eval model instead of destroying it?
result: stopped at ~step 45/500: acc 1.4-2.2%, gnorm 0.31-0.42, 55% of groups degenerate
finding: The anti-collapse fixes hold: 45 steps flat with a stable gradient norm, against the previous run that fell 32%->11% over 500. But there is nothing to amplify - sampled accuracy on the RL set is 1.4-2.2% at T=0.9 while the same checkpoint scores 31% greedy on the same distribution, and 55% of groups are all-wrong or all-correct so half the compute produces zero gradient. An independent 22-agent audit of 119 problems put the gold error rate at 0.84%, so this is genuine difficulty, not broken rewards.
decision: No RL until SFT clears roughly 60% on math-500 and pass@8 minus pass@1 is a real gap. GPUs go to the first SFT run on the repaired pipeline: holdout exclusion, corrected gold-answer extraction, greedy packing, fixed step verifier, dt_bias init, training-time softcap, short_conv LR group.

name: k4_11b_0827
notes: 8xH20 batch 24 no grad_ckpt, FP8 (torchao), doc_mask on, AttnRes Block-4 with the gain folded into the query; mix 11.5B tokens over web 8.31B / en 0.20B / math 0.16B / code 0.08B / chat 0.04B, anneal last 10% with math 4.0% -> 28.3%; 14606 steps at 82K tok/s/gpu = ~4.9h
hypothesis: First pretrain on the repaired pipeline and the new architecture, from scratch. Everything upstream changed at once, so the number that decides this run is post-SFT math-hard against the old base's 3.1%, not the pretrain loss against any earlier curve. What changed: fineweb-2 added (its source path had never resolved), 59% of it converted from Traditional to Simplified, the eval-holdout leak through the QA join closed (746 contaminated docs, 496 of the 500 math-500 questions), the domain mix sized to the corpus that exists and rebalanced so the anneal actually receives math, AttnRes enabled for the first time in a completed run, and batch dropped from 72 to 24 so gradient checkpointing is off (2.4x throughput).

name: k4_11b_lr05
notes: 8xH20 batch 24 no grad_ckpt, FP8, doc_mask, AttnRes Block-4 (gain folded), lr_scale 0.5; mix 11.5B tokens, anneal math 4.0->28.3%; 14606 steps
hypothesis: Same run as k4_11b_0827 with every optimizer lr halved. That run's loss bottomed at 3.447 by step 610 then climbed to 4.359 by 1060 with val 3.03->3.56, at a constant peak lr: too large a step for 786K tokens per update, 2.25x smaller than the batch these nanochat rates were tuned for. Does halving hold the descent past step 1000, or is the instability AttnRes rather than the lr?

name: pretrain_k3_v2
hypothesis: Does the K3 hybrid (KDA + Gated MLA, hd=128) train stably in native FP8 at 206M?
finding: Yes — 2.26B tokens, 3 epochs, no NaN. FP8 e4m3 both directions is stable as long as activation checkpointing is on (root cause of that dependency found later, see perf_sweep).
decision: K3 becomes the base for every downstream stage; ckpt_k3-mla_2b_step2000.pt is the only valid pretrain checkpoint (the old ckpt.pt is a different architecture and will not load).

name: sft_stage1
hypothesis: What does the model score on Chinese grade-school math after a normal instruction SFT?
finding: 32.2% on the 500-problem holdout. The CoT is fluent and well-formed; the arithmetic inside it is wrong. Fluency and correctness are decoupled at this scale.
decision: Treat 32.2% as the number every later experiment must beat. Stop reading loss as progress — only holdout accuracy counts.

name: sft_math_stage2
hypothesis: Does a second SFT pass on math-only data lift math accuracy?
finding: No — 32.2%, unchanged. Stage-1 had already seen all of school_math, so stage-2 added no information, only more passes over the same rows.
decision: Stop doing stage-2 passes over data stage-1 already contains. New capability needs new data, not more epochs.

name: sft_short_stage2
hypothesis: Is the DeepSeek-style 'restate then rewrite' answer format what is holding accuracy back?
finding: No — 31.6%. The format did change (output halved in length, no second rewrite, boxed rate near 100%) but accuracy did not move. Format is a token-efficiency lever, not an accuracy lever.
decision: Keep the short format for cheaper generation and cleaner verification, but stop expecting accuracy from formatting work.

name: rlvr_stage2
hypothesis: Can GRPO with a verifiable boxed reward lift a 32% model?
finding: No — collapsed to 11.2%. Three causes, none of them the choice of RL algorithm: T=0.1 made the 8 samples per prompt near-identical so most groups had std=0 and zero advantage; there was no KL term or reference model, so 500 steps drifted unanchored; and at 32% pass@1 there was little gap between pass@1 and pass@8 for RL to amplify.
decision: No RL until SFT clears ~60% and pass@8 minus pass@1 is at least 15 points. When RL resumes: sequence-level ratio (GSPO), T around 0.8, KL beta 0.01-0.04, and only train on prompts with a 20-80% solve rate (the LFM-1.3B-Math selection rule).

name: sft_v2_stage1
hypothesis: Redo stage-1 from the pretrain checkpoint using only verified short-format data — better than the original mix?
finding: No — 26.4%. The rebuilt mix dropped openo1 (77K) and the full-length school_math_r1_zh (223K) in exchange for 110K filtered rows. Filtering raised per-row quality and lowered total information; accuracy followed the total, not the quality.
decision: Never let a quality filter shrink the corpus without replacing the volume. Verify aggressively, then backfill to at least the original token count.

name: sft_v5_hard
finding: The hard eval separates checkpoints that math-500 cannot: v4 scored 0.8% and v5 3.1% there, while on math-500 they are 32.0% vs 31.0% (indistinguishable). Absolute level is still near-zero — the model gets almost every arithmetic step wrong on L3/L4.
decision: math_hard_eval_1k is now the primary metric; math-500 is kept only as a regression tripwire.

name: rlvr_gspo
result: stopped at step 90/500: acc 1.6-2.3%, gnorm 0.35-0.43, ~30% of groups degenerate
finding: A second copy of the run survived the first stop (duplicate launch on port 29541) and got to step 90 — 90 steps of flat accuracy with a stable gradient norm confirms the anti-collapse fixes hold, and equally confirms there is no signal to amplify: 1.6-2.3% sampled at T=0.9 against 31% greedy on the same distribution from the same checkpoint. Gold quality is not the cause (22-agent audit: 0.84% bad).
decision: Abandon RL on the old architecture. Pivot to a fresh pretrain on the new architecture (AttnRes + fused GEMMs + doc_mask + domain mix), because a 31%-greedy/2%-sampled base has no exploitable pass@k gap regardless of the RL objective.

name: ab2_attnres_vs_base
notes: 8xH20, batch 72, flat 2.26B token cache, same seed, 500 steps each = 1.18B tokens/arm
hypothesis: Does Attention Residuals (softmax over depth instead of the residual sum) actually lower loss at 200M/L=12, and what does it cost in throughput? The earlier base-only arm ran on stale code (no doc_mask, old dt_bias init, short_conv in the wrong LR group), so both arms are re-run on current code to make the comparison mean anything.
result: both arms died at 2m43s: CUDA OOM, 94.9/95.2 GiB on every rank
finding: The A/B never ran; what it found instead is that Cfg.batch=72 with Cfg.grad_ckpt=False does not fit on an H20 at all. Batch 48 OOMs identically (93.5 GiB), so the earlier 6-GPU ablation_base that reached 500 steps at batch 72 must have run the pod's older train.py, back when grad_ckpt still defaulted to True — the default was flipped to False without re-measuring what batch that leaves room for.
decision: Ablations move to --grad_ckpt. An adversarial review then measured that Full AttnRes at L=12 makes Inductor save one [B,T,D] tensor per (consumer, source) pair — 325 of them, 196 GB/GPU at batch 72 — so the sweep now compares base / attn_res_blocks=4 / attn_res_blocks=2 / Full rather than assuming Full is affordable.

name: doc_mask_ab
hypothesis: Does --doc_mask (default ON since d5db37b) actually work on GPU, and what does the varlen FlashKDA path cost? It had never been run on a GPU, and the concern was a torch.compile recompile storm from the per-batch cu_seqlens length plus the FlashKDA 'A_log must be float32' error on the varlen path.
result: no_doc_mask 9m04s / docmask 8m18s, both exit 0, both 32 recompiles
finding: doc_mask is free. mark_dynamic(cu, 0) does its job: the two arms recompile exactly the same number of times, so the varying cu_seqlens length triggers nothing. The 32 recompiles come from Block.forward specializing on mixer type (guard: ___check_type_id(self._modules['mixer']) type=DeltaRecurrence), which is 2 variants over 12 layers and is unrelated to doc_mask. No FlashKDA A_log error — the .float() patch is still in the pod's site-packages, which is itself the risk: it is not in the repo and dies with the container.
decision: Keep doc_mask ON for the pretrain. Neither arm's wall-clock is a throughput measurement — both were dominated by compile and by the epoch-end validation, which is what led to capping that validation at Cfg.val_batches_full.

name: throughput_bisect
hypothesis: The first 8-GPU run measured 37K tok/s/gpu at MFU 15% against runs/ablation_base.log's 91K at MFU 38%, which would turn a 4.4h pretrain into 10.8h. Was that a real regression introduced between aa3a8b9 and HEAD, and if so which change?
result: no regression; batch 32 without grad_ckpt = 90K tok/s/gpu MFU 38%, batch 72 with grad_ckpt = 37K MFU 15%
finding: There was no regression. Checking out aa3a8b9 -- the commit that produced the 91K figure -- and running it at its own committed Cfg (batch 72, grad_ckpt False) OOMs on 8xH20 exactly like HEAD, so 91K cannot have come from the configuration it was being compared against; the pod's working copy at the time must have carried different values. Three suspects were eliminated on the way, each worth knowing on its own: doc_mask is free (36K with, 37K without, and it is not what exhausts memory -- batch 72 without grad_ckpt OOMs with doc_mask off too); GPU count is not it (6 GPUs give 37K/gpu, same as 8); and grad_ckpt is not independently slow. What is true is that Cfg.batch=72 has never fit without gradient checkpointing at 206M/seq4096 on a 95GB card -- it needs >95GB against 52GB with checkpointing -- and that paying for checkpointing to keep a large batch costs 2.4x, while simply shrinking the batch costs nothing: 90K at batch 32, 89K at 24, 84K at 16.
decision: Pretrain at batch 32 (or the largest batch that still fits with AttnRes) with grad_ckpt OFF. Cfg.batch's default of 72 is a trap -- it silently forces the slow path -- and its comment claiming 97GB is enough is wrong. Separately: comparing a throughput number against a log whose configuration was never recorded cost about 90 minutes; runs/*.log gets no config header because it is written by runlog while the header goes through print.

name: rl_direct
notes: GSPO, group 8, T=0.9, KL 0.02, prompts filtered to the 20-80% solve-rate band
hypothesis: The previous RL run had nothing to amplify: 30-55% of groups were all-right or all-wrong, so half the compute produced no gradient. With prompts restricted to the band this model actually solves 20-80% of the time, does accuracy move at all?
finding: Direct RL on the base is a near-null: math-500 +0.8 over base (52.4 vs 51.6, within noise), math-hard flat at 2.9%, and pass@8 DROPPED 3-4.6 points (7.0% vs the base's 10.1-11.6%) -- the one frontier where the base was strongest. The run nearly died mid-way: RL-set acc peaked 0.668 at step 280, collapsed to 0.339 by step 390 (loss x120, generation time 44s->152s as generations ran to the 320-token cap), then recovered to 0.645 by 500. The SFT+RL path never had this excursion -- SFT's compressed generations (40-char median vs the base's 104) leave no room to run away, so SFT regularizes the RL loop even though its own weights are worse. The base's wider pass@8 gap (+10.1% vs +5.4%) did not translate into more amplification: the band was 1048 problems, comparable to the SFT run's, but the recovery overfit to band easy wins and narrowed sampling diversity. Workflow forensics (same day): gen-time runaway LED the collapse (44s->158s, lockstep with the acc drop, loss x122 lagged 40-60 steps); gnorm and degen were passengers (degen fell during the crash). The recovery to 0.645 was a noisy overfit equilibrium, not restored capability -- pass@1 recovered while pass@8 fell, the signature of output-distribution mode narrowing that weight diffs cannot see. The base's broad output distribution is unstable under on-policy RL; SFT's length compression is an implicit regularizer. Separately: the band sits inside the capability envelope (easy parametrizations of L3/L4 programs), so RL only polishes pass@k->pass@1 -- the transfer ceiling for BOTH runs.
decision: Keep SFT+RL as production (math-hard 4.1% still best). Next in order: (1) best-ckpt saving DONE (40fa735); (2) length-only SFT -- compress base generations to ~40 chars median, no math content -- then RL with KL 0.05: isolates compression as the active ingredient; (3) KL sweep 0.05/0.1; (4) band curriculum toward hard parametrizations (reverse reasoning, big numbers, multi-constraint) to break the transfer ceiling. DAPO resampling deprioritized: degen was a passenger, not the cause.

name: sft_k4
result: math-500 39.2% (196/500); math-hard deferred to the bench stage
finding: First break from the 32% plateau: four SFT runs on the 2.26B-token base landed at 32.2 / 26.8 / 32.0 / 31.0, and this one is 39.2% off an 11.5B-token base. The number is also more trustworthy than those four, which were measured against a holdout that had 496 of its 500 questions sitting in the training corpus with full solutions -- that leak was closed today, so 39.2% is a measurement where 32% was partly recall.
decision: math-hard against the old base's 3.1% is still the number that decides whether the pretrain was worth it; math-500 is saturated by design and CLAUDE.md already says not to conclude from it. Proceed to the solve-rate probe.

name: rl_k4
finding: RL works, and the difficulty filter is why. Restricting prompts to the 20-80% solve-rate band cut degenerate groups from 30-55% to 3% at the start, and accuracy on the RL set rose 0.489 -> 0.653 over 500 steps; it transferred, taking math-hard 3.2% -> 4.1%, the first time that metric has moved off ~3% across four SFT runs and three RL attempts. But RL could not repay what SFT had cost: 44.6% on math-500 against the base's 51.6%.
decision: Drop the SFT stage and run RL directly on the pretrain base. SFT is now measurably harmful here -- see the sft_k4 record -- and the base has both the higher starting point (51.6% / 2.9%) and the wider pass@8 gap (+10.1% vs +5.4%), which is the quantity RL amplifies.

name: k4_11b_lr05
finding: The anneal did the SFT stage's job, better than SFT did. 28.3% math in the last 10% of tokens -- 435K examples in the same 问：/答：\\boxed{} shape the eval uses -- left the raw base at 51.6% on math-500, against 31.0% for the old base AFTER supervised fine-tuning. Format came with it: 91.6% of the base's math-hard generations are answer-parseable, higher than the 88.2% after SFT. What the anneal did not buy is hard-problem ability: math-hard is 2.9%, the same ~3% the old pipeline reached.
decision: This checkpoint, not the SFT one, is the base for everything downstream.
